title: Two-slot rings in UB and GM, with the GM round trip ordered by hand
surface: DBuff(f32, [1, 64], Position.UB) indexed by beat; GMBuff(f32, [1, 64], slots=2, per_core=False) as a GM workspace ring; SEvent(Pipe.MTE3, Pipe.MTE2) set and waited inside auto_sync(); one kernel(mode="vec") launch
study_for: What `auto_sync()` does and does not cover. It orders everything on chip, including the reuse of both UB rings. It does not order a round trip through GM, so the MTE3 write and the MTE2 read back are ordered by an explicit `SEvent(Pipe.MTE3, Pipe.MTE2)` -- naming exactly the two pipes involved.

Five beats over two slots, on purpose. The rings wrap twice and the fifth beat takes slot 0 for the third time, so a kernel that reused a slot still in flight has an opportunity to do so. A four-beat version would not reach that third reuse.

A `GMBuff` with `per_core=False` is one workspace shared by the launch rather than one per core. With a single vector core that distinction changes nothing here, which is exactly why it is worth reading before copying into a kernel where there are several.

The answer is a copy, which is the point: any ordering mistake shows up as a whole row in the wrong place rather than as a small numeric difference. The rows are ten apart by construction, `check_domain` asserts that separation, and `compare` reports which source row each wrong row actually came from.
do_not_copy_when: You have more than one core and a shared GM workspace. `per_core=False` means one ring for the launch; with several cores writing it, the ownership question this example never asks becomes the whole problem.
You are relying on autosync for a GM round trip. It does not order one. The event here is not decoration.
Your slot count divides your beat count evenly. Then no slot is ever reused while another is in flight in the way the fifth beat does here, and the reuse this example is about is not being exercised.
